pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 5-6 (Reception/Y1). Fluently add and subtract within 5 — quick, accurate recall/near-recall of the small facts (2+3, 5−2). The first fluency milestone (centrality 0.18); small enough to be subitised and memorised, it seeds automaticity for all later mental calculation.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y1): number bonds and related facts within 20; the small facts within 5 are the foundational subset built first.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): K.OA.5 'fluently add and subtract within 5'.
• Operational details — Fluency = efficient, accurate, flexible — NOT speed alone. Build it from subitising (instantly seeing quantities to 5) and part-whole knowledge, so recall is meaningful, then use short, frequent, low-stakes retrieval practice to firm it up. Include subtraction alongside addition and the +0 case. Avoid anxiety-inducing timed drill as the primary mechanism; interleave strategy talk with quick recall.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 5): subitise quantities to 5 and answer within-5 additions with minimal counting. Tier B (age 5-6): answer any within-5 addition or subtraction quickly, from recall or a fast strategy. Tier C (age 6): recall within-5 facts automatically and use them to reason (e.g. 5−2 from 2+3).
bestPractices: Build fluency FROM subitising and part-whole understanding rather than rote drill — children who can instantly see 4 as 3-and-1 recall the facts meaningfully.
Use short, frequent, low-stakes retrieval practice (a few minutes daily) rather than long high-pressure timed tests, which can induce maths anxiety without improving learning.
Interleave addition and its inverse subtraction, and include +0/−0, so the small-fact set is complete and connected.
Represent facts on fingers, five-frames and dice/domino patterns so recall is anchored to instantly-recognisable images.
Treat fluency as accuracy + efficiency + flexibility (choosing a good strategy), not merely answering fast.
keyRepresentations: Five-frame and finger patterns for subitising quantities to 5
Number track 0-5 for counting-on/back where needed
Fact cards / quick-image flashes for retrieval practice
commonMisconceptions: Counting from 1 on fingers for every fact, never moving to recall — fluency stalls.
Equating fluency with speed and rushing, producing errors, or freezing under time pressure.
Knowing additions but not the related subtractions within 5.
Uncertainty with 0 (thinking 3 + 0 must change the number).
Over-reliance on one strategy (always counting on) rather than recognising known facts.

learn.summary: Help children aged 5-6 become fluent at adding and subtracting within 5 (e.g. 2+3, 5-2, 3-3, 4+0), where fluency means accurate, efficient and flexible recall built from subitising and part-whole understanding — not raw speed. The primary engine is short, frequent, low-stakes retrieval practice with quantity images (five-frames, dice/domino patterns, fingers) kept attached until recall is secure, interleaving addition with its inverse subtraction and including the +0/-0 case.

activities.title: Quick-flash fact practice from a dot pattern
feedback: If the child counts every dot (or finger) from one on each item, do NOT ban finger-counting or mark it wrong — it is a normal stage; keep exposure short and frequent, as regular subitising practice can help recall become more secure over time.
If addition is instant but subtraction is counted (2 + 3 fast, 5 − 2 slow), link the subtraction to the known addition fact as a fact family and give brief targeted subtraction practice.
If the child gives 3 for 3 − 3, or queries/refuses a zero result, act out taking all away (and adding nothing) with real objects to establish 0 as a legitimate answer.
Praise fast AND accurate recall; if the child rushes and makes errors, slow down and re-attach the pattern image rather than pushing for speed alone.
activities.rationale: Retrieval practice is the mechanism for automaticity, and anchoring facts to subitisable images (five-frames, dice, fingers) makes the recall meaningful and flexible. An adaptive flash format that speeds up on success and re-shows the image on error blends seeing with recall while keeping stakes low.
sourceClaims: Within-5 (and within-20) number facts are built for fluent recall in Y1, from number bonds and related facts.
Fluency is accuracy, efficiency and flexibility built from strategies and subitising; frequent low-stakes retrieval beats high-pressure timed drill, which can cause maths anxiety.
learnerActions: A five-frame, dice or domino pattern (e.g. four dots) appears briefly, then the child says or taps the answer to a fact tied to it (e.g. 4 + 1, or 5 − 1 from the same image).
Keep answering a short daily set of items in a few minutes, mixing addition and subtraction.
When a fact is answered quickly and correctly, show the image more briefly next time; when the child hesitates or errs, re-show the pattern longer and talk through what they see.
Include zero cases such as 4 + 0 and 3 − 3 in the mix.
activities.intendedInsight: A child can stop counting dots one by one and simply KNOW a pattern's value, then flip the same image into a subtraction (5 − 1 = 4). Recall becomes meaningful because it is anchored to an instantly-recognisable quantity image.

activities.title: Periodic low-stakes fact check
feedback: Keep stakes low and framing calm; a check that feels like a high-pressure timed test can induce anxiety without improving learning.
Use the results to target the specific lagging facts (often subtractions) with more flash practice, rather than repeating everything.
activities.rationale: A short fact check is an honest probe of automaticity and complements daily retrieval practice, but a fixed linear item set is less adaptive and can feel high-stakes, so it suits periodic use rather than as the main practice engine. Recognition-format items confirm what is recalled but do not by themselves build automaticity.
sourceClaims: Fluency is accuracy, efficiency and flexibility built from strategies and subitising; frequent low-stakes retrieval beats high-pressure timed drill, which can cause maths anxiety.
learnerActions: Work through a short set of image-supported fact items (multiple-choice or fill-the-blank) that interleave addition and subtraction within 5, including a zero case.
Treat this as an occasional check of what has become automatic, not the daily practice engine.
After answering, note which facts were known instantly and which were worked out.
activities.intendedInsight: Children and adults can see which within-5 facts are now recalled automatically and which still need practice, especially any subtraction or zero facts that lag.

activities.title: Oral quick-fire warm-up and subitising reference
feedback: If the child counts from one or hesitates, point to the matching dot/five-frame pattern rather than correcting the answer harshly.
A static pattern reference supports recognition but cannot by itself drive the repeated retrieval that fluency needs, so pair it with the flash practice.
activities.rationale: Oral quick-fire and strategy talk interleave recall with reasoning and surface children's strategies, while a static subitising reference anchors recall to instantly-recognisable images; both support the main retrieval practice without replacing it.
sourceClaims: Fluency is accuracy, efficiency and flexibility built from strategies and subitising; frequent low-stakes retrieval beats high-pressure timed drill, which can cause maths anxiety.
learnerActions: Run a brief spoken quick-fire: 'What's 2 and 3? … 5 take away 2? … 4 and 1? … 3 take away 3?' and have the child answer aloud fast.
Ask follow-up reasoning prompts: 'Which of those did you just know, and which did you work out?', 'If 2 + 3 = 5, what is 5 − 3?', 'What happens if I add 0 to 4?'
Keep a reference chart of subitisable patterns 0-5 (five-frames, dice/dot patterns) visible to glance at when recall is uncertain.
activities.intendedInsight: Talking through which facts were known versus worked out surfaces the move from counting to recall, and connects each subtraction to its related addition.

constraints: Fluency means accuracy + efficiency + flexibility (choosing a good strategy), not speed alone; avoid making timed drill the primary mechanism, as time pressure can induce maths anxiety without improving learning.
Do not ban or penalise finger-counting from one — it is a normal developmental stage that, for many children, gives way to recall with regular short subitising and retrieval practice.
Build recall FROM subitising and part-whole understanding, not rote drill, so facts are meaningful; keep the quantity image attached until recall is secure.
Always interleave subtraction with addition and include the +0/-0 case so the small-fact set is complete and connected.

A static dot/five-frame reference aids recognition but cannot by itself drive repeated retrieval; oral quick-fire struggles to deliver enough varied fast reps, so each works best alongside frequent short practice.
A recognition-only check (multiple-choice) confirms what is recalled but does not by itself build automaticity; use it periodically, not as the daily engine.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original claimed an adaptive flash game grows fluency 'in a way a fixed medium cannot' and rated a static image and oral dialogue as weaker; these are catalog fit judgements, not established comparative efficacy. Treated here as a reasonable design proposal with stated affordances/limits rather than a universal law.

Of the cited sources, only the DfE National Curriculum claim is marked verified; the CCSS K.OA.5 and the Baroody/Boaler/NCETM claims are marked unverified in the source row and should not be read as independently confirmed. The CCSS K.OA.5 claim is not used as an activity sourceClaim because it only restates the objective/topic rather than supporting a teaching principle; the retained DfE claim is partly a curriculum statement and only indirectly supports the retrieval-practice rationale.

Self-audit of the facts used: 2+3=5, 5-2=3, 4+1=5, 3-3=0, 5-1=4, 5-3=2, 3+0=3, 4+0=4 all check out; the diagnostic/correct-answer set (5, 3, 5, 0) is consistent. The 5 − 1 = 4 fact tied to a four-dot image is coherent with the four-dot pattern shown.

probeDeeper: Which of those did you just know, and which did you work out?
What is 3 take away 3 — how can there be none left?
What happens if I add 0 to 4?
assess.correctAnswer: 5, 3, 5, 0 — answered quickly from recall or subitising, without laborious counting from one.

errorPatterns.pattern: Still counts all on fingers from one rather than recalling within-5 facts.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT ban finger-counting or mark it wrong — recall automates with regular short exposure and subitising practice; it is a normal stage.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Audible or visible counting from one on every item.

errorPatterns.pattern: Mishandles zero — gives 3 − 3 as 3, or thinks an operation must change the number.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Act out taking all away (and adding nothing) with objects to establish 0 as a legitimate result.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child answers 3 for 3 − 3, or refuses/queries a zero result.

errorPatterns.pattern: Addition secure but subtraction lags — 2 + 3 instant, 5 − 2 counted.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Link subtraction to the known addition fact (fact families); brief targeted subtraction practice.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Clear asymmetry between fluent adds and slow subtractions.

responseLevels.gap: Counts all from one on most items, or mishandles zero.
responseLevels.full: Answers all within-5 facts, including zero cases, quickly and accurately from recall.
responseLevels.partial: Recalls some facts quickly but others (often subtraction) are still counted.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Quick answers, try not to count on your fingers: what is 2 + 3? … 5 − 2? … 4 + 1? … 3 − 3?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watch for quick recall / subitising versus counting on fingers from one. Fluency within 5 means fast AND accurate with minimal counting. The 3 − 3 item also catches whether zero as a result is understood.
